facts.claim: Confederate artillery opened fire on Fort Sumter, starting the Civil War
facts.context: The bombardment of the federal fort in Charleston Harbor began before dawn on April 12, 1861. The garrison surrendered the next day.
facts.goDeeper: Nobody was killed by enemy fire during the battle. The only deaths came from an accidental cannon explosion during the surrender ceremony.

facts.claim: Abraham Lincoln was assassinated
facts.context: John Wilkes Booth shot Lincoln at Ford's Theatre on April 14, 1865. Lincoln died the next morning, five days after Lee's surrender.
facts.goDeeper: Booth's original plan was to kidnap Lincoln and ransom him for Confederate prisoners. He only switched to murder after the Confederacy collapsed.

facts.claim: The Battle of Gettysburg was fought
facts.context: Three days of fighting in Pennsylvania, July 1-3, 1863, ended Lee's second invasion of the North.
facts.goDeeper: Lee never again mounted a strategic offensive into Union territory after Gettysburg.

facts.claim: Length of the Gettysburg Address
facts.context: Lincoln's speech ran about 270 words and took roughly two minutes to deliver.
facts.goDeeper: The main speaker that day, Edward Everett, talked for two hours. Almost nobody remembers a word of it.

facts.claim: The Emancipation Proclamation took legal effect
facts.context: Lincoln issued a preliminary proclamation in September 1862; the final order took effect January 1, 1863.
facts.goDeeper: It applied only to territory in rebellion, so it freed nobody in the loyal slave states of Kentucky, Delaware, Maryland or Missouri.

facts.claim: Robert E. Lee surrendered to Grant at Appomattox Court House
facts.context: The surrender took place on April 9, 1865, effectively ending the war in the East.
facts.goDeeper: Other Confederate armies kept fighting for weeks. The last significant surrender came in late June 1865.

facts.claim: Total casualties at the Battle of Antietam
facts.context: September 17, 1862 produced roughly 22,000 killed, wounded and missing, making it the bloodiest single day in American history.
facts.goDeeper: The battle was tactically a draw, but it gave Lincoln the victory he needed to announce the Emancipation Proclamation.

facts.claim: Number of states that joined the Confederacy
facts.context: Seven states seceded before Lincoln took office; four more followed after Fort Sumter.
facts.goDeeper: The western counties of Virginia refused to secede and split off to become the new state of West Virginia in 1863.

facts.claim: Abraham Lincoln's age when he died
facts.context: Born February 12, 1809, Lincoln died April 15, 1865, two months past his 56th birthday.
facts.goDeeper: He was the first American president to be assassinated, and the tallest at 6 feet 4 inches.

facts.claim: Traditional estimate of total deaths in the Civil War
facts.context: The long-standing figure is about 620,000 dead on both sides. More recent demographic work pushes the estimate as high as 750,000.
facts.goDeeper: Roughly two-thirds of those deaths came from disease rather than combat.

facts.claim: The Thirteenth Amendment abolishing slavery was ratified
facts.context: Congress passed it in January 1865 and the states completed ratification on December 6, 1865, months after the war ended.
facts.goDeeper: Mississippi did not symbolically ratify the amendment until 1995, and the paperwork was not filed until 2013.

source.title: Thirteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution

facts.claim: The First Battle of Bull Run was fought
facts.context: The first major land battle, on July 21, 1861, ended in a Union rout near Manassas, Virginia.
facts.goDeeper: Washington civilians rode out with picnic baskets to watch, then got caught in the retreat.

facts.claim: Sherman captured Atlanta
facts.context: Confederate forces evacuated on September 1-2, 1864 after a summer-long campaign.
facts.goDeeper: The news almost certainly saved Lincoln's re-election that November, which had looked doubtful all summer.

facts.claim: Vicksburg surrendered to Grant, giving the Union control of the Mississippi
facts.context: The city fell on July 4, 1863, the day after Gettysburg ended.
facts.goDeeper: Vicksburg reportedly did not celebrate the Fourth of July again for another eighty years.

facts.claim: Abraham Lincoln was first elected president
facts.context: Lincoln won the November 1860 election with under 40 percent of the popular vote in a four-way race.
facts.goDeeper: He was not even on the ballot in ten Southern states.

facts.claim: The ironclads Monitor and Virginia fought at Hampton Roads
facts.context: The first battle between ironclad warships took place March 8-9, 1862 and ended inconclusively.
facts.goDeeper: The engagement made every wooden navy in the world obsolete almost overnight.

facts.claim: The Battle of Shiloh was fought in Tennessee
facts.context: Fought April 6-7, 1862, Shiloh shocked both sides with casualties higher than all previous American battles combined.
facts.goDeeper: Grant was nearly relieved of command afterward for being caught unprepared on the first day.

facts.claim: Robert E. Lee was offered a senior command in the Union army before he joined the Confederacy
facts.context: In April 1861 Lee was offered command of the field forces being raised to suppress the rebellion. He declined and resigned when Virginia seceded.
facts.goDeeper: Lee had spent 32 years in the U.S. Army and had called secession 'nothing but revolution' in a letter that January.

facts.claim: The Emancipation Proclamation freed every enslaved person in the United States
facts.context: It applied only to areas still in rebellion. Slavery in the loyal border states was not ended until the Thirteenth Amendment.
facts.goDeeper: Because it was issued as a war measure against enemy territory, its legal basis was Lincoln's power as commander in chief, not an act of Congress.

facts.claim: Ulysses S. Grant commanded all Union armies from the beginning of the war
facts.context: Grant was made general-in-chief of all Union armies in March 1864, nearly three years into the war. He started it as a colonel of Illinois volunteers.
facts.goDeeper: Grant had left the army in 1854 under a cloud and was working in his family's leather goods store in Galena, Illinois when the war broke out.
